excerpt: Symptoms, prescriptions and dosage: the phrases that matter most when you feel unwell.

body_html:
Knowing what to say at the pharmacy in Spanish matters, because it is usually the first place you go when you feel unwell abroad or need to help a Spanish-speaking relative. In Mexico, Spain and much of Latin America, pharmacists give a lot of advice, and many common medicines are sold over the counter. You need to describe your symptoms, ask what to take and understand the dosage. Here are the phrases for each step, with the safety questions you should always ask.

Quick answer
  • Start: Buenas tardes. ¿Me podría recomendar algo para la tos?
  • Symptoms: Me duele la cabeza. Tengo fiebre.
  • Safety: Soy alérgico a la penicilina. ¿Tiene efectos secundarios?
  • Dosage: ¿Cada cuánto lo tomo? ¿Con o sin comida?
{{toc}}

Describing your symptoms

SpanishEnglish
Me duele la cabeza.I have a headache.
Me duele el estómago.I have a stomachache.
Me duele la garganta.I have a sore throat.
Tengo fiebre.I have a fever.
Tengo tos.I have a cough.
Tengo gripa.I have the flu. (Mexico; Spain: Tengo gripe)
Estoy mareado.I feel dizzy.
Tengo diarrea.I have diarrhea.
Me pica la piel.My skin is itchy.
Me quemé con el sol.I got sunburned.

Doler works like {{link:how-to-use-gustar|gustar}}: the body part is the subject. Me duele la cabeza (one thing hurts), me duelen los pies (my feet hurt).

Asking for medicine at the pharmacy in Spanish

  • ¿Me podría recomendar algo para el dolor de cabeza? Could you recommend something for a headache?
  • ¿Tiene algo para la alergia? Do you have something for allergies?
  • Busco un jarabe para la tos. I’m looking for a cough syrup.
  • ¿Necesito receta para esto? Do I need a prescription for this?
  • ¿Tiene la versión genérica? Do you have the generic version?

Useful product words: pastillas (pills), cápsulas (capsules), jarabe (syrup), pomada or crema (ointment), gotas (drops), curitas (Band-Aids in Mexico; tiritas in Spain).

{{image:2}}

Safety questions to always ask

These questions protect you, whatever your level of Spanish:

  • Soy alérgico a… I’m allergic to… (alérgica if you are female)
  • Estoy tomando otro medicamento. ¿Lo puedo combinar? I’m taking another medicine. Can I combine them?
  • Estoy embarazada. I’m pregnant. (This is where embarazada is exactly the right word.)
  • ¿Tiene efectos secundarios? Does it have side effects?
  • ¿Da sueño? Does it make you drowsy?
  • ¿Es para niños? Is it suitable for children?

If anything is unclear, ask the pharmacist to write it down: ¿Me lo puede escribir, por favor?

Understanding the dosage

SpanishEnglish
Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas.Take one pill every eight hours.
Dos veces al día.Twice a day.
Con alimentos.With food.
En ayunas.On an empty stomach.
Antes de dormir.Before bed.
No más de tres al día.No more than three a day.
Durante cinco días.For five days.

To check you understood, repeat it back: Entonces, una cada ocho horas, con comida, ¿verdad? So, one every eight hours, with food, right?

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Buying for someone else

Often you are at the pharmacy for a child, a partner or an older relative. Make it clear who the medicine is for: Es para mi hijo de cinco años (It’s for my five-year-old son). Es para mi mamá, tiene setenta años (It’s for my mom, she’s seventy). The pharmacist will usually ask the person’s age and weight for children, so it helps to know the weight in kilos: Pesa veinte kilos (He weighs twenty kilos). Always check the dose on the label with the pharmacist before giving a medicine to a child.

A sample conversation at the pharmacy

Tú: Buenas tardes. Tengo mucha tos y me duele la garganta.
Good afternoon. I have a bad cough and a sore throat.

Farmacéutica: ¿Tiene fiebre? ¿Desde cuándo?
Do you have a fever? Since when?

Tú: No, fiebre no. Desde hace dos días.
No fever. For two days now.

Farmacéutica: Le recomiendo este jarabe. Una cucharada cada ocho horas.
I recommend this syrup. One spoonful every eight hours.

Tú: ¿Da sueño? Tengo que manejar.
Does it make you drowsy? I have to drive.

Farmacéutica: No, este no. Pero si no mejora en tres días, vaya al médico.
No, not this one. But if you don’t get better in three days, see a doctor.

{{image:3}}

Pharmacies in Mexico, Spain and the US

Mexico: many pharmacies have a small doctor’s office next door (consultorio) where you can see a doctor for a low fee. Antibiotics require a prescription. Spain: pharmacies are marked by a green cross, and one in each area stays open at night (farmacia de guardia). United States: many pharmacies offer service in Spanish; ask ¿Hay alguien que hable español?

For anything serious, see a doctor; my guide to {{link:at-the-doctor-in-spanish|the doctor’s office in Spanish}} covers the appointment itself, and {{link:emergency-phrases-in-spanish|emergency phrases in Spanish}} covers urgent situations. For trustworthy health information in Spanish, the MedlinePlus en español site from the US National Library of Medicine is reliable.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Being able to speak at the pharmacy in Spanish gives you real peace of mind. Describe your symptoms with me duele and tengo, always mention allergies and other medicines, and repeat the dosage back before you leave. For other everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do I ask for medicine in Spanish?
faq.a: Say ¿Me podría recomendar algo para…? followed by the problem, for example la tos or el dolor de cabeza.

faq.q: How do you say “I’m allergic to” in Spanish?
faq.a: Soy alérgico a… (male) or soy alérgica a… (female).

faq.q: Do I need a prescription in Mexican pharmacies?
faq.a: For many common medicines, no, but antibiotics and some other medicines require a prescription.

faq.q: How do I ask how often to take a medicine?
faq.a: ¿Cada cuánto lo tomo? or ¿Cuántas veces al día?

questions.explain: Doler works like gustar: the head hurts you.
A plural subject needs a plural verb.
Dar sueño means to make someone sleepy.
Vendas are bandages; curitas are adhesive strips.
